title: Neural attention
matchup: Bahdanau, Cho & Bengio (2014) and Larochelle & Hinton (2010) vs Schmidhuber & Huber (1990-91) and Schmidhuber (1991-93)
question: Do Schmidhuber's 1990-93 systems establish priority for the neural attention mechanisms described in the 2010 and 2014 papers?

usual_credit.summary: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2014) are usually credited with attention for neural machine translation, in which a decoder learns a soft alignment over the encoder's states instead of relying on one fixed vector. The ACM's 2019 Turing Award announcement says Bengio's group introduced an attention mechanism that led to breakthroughs in machine translation. For glimpse-based visual attention, Larochelle and Hinton (2010) and Mnih et al. (2014) are the commonly cited systems.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber says two forms of neural attention already existed in his lab by 1990-93. The first was 'hard' attention in observation space, where a reinforcement-learning controller steers an artificial fovea (Schmidhuber and Huber, 1990-91), and the second was 'soft' attention in the latent space of fast weight programmers, whose 1993 recurrent extension spoke of learning 'internal spotlights of attention'. He says the 2010 and 2014 papers did not cite this work, and that Hinton, whom he describes as the reviewer of his 1990 paper, later called his own 2010 system the first of its kind. The soft-attention part of the claim overlaps with the Transformer dispute.

response.summary: Larochelle and Hinton's 2010 paper claims the first implemented system jointly training its recognition and fixation components, which is narrower than priority for all neural attention. In an email dated September 2022 and [published by Andrej Karpathy](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1864023344435380613) in December 2024, Bahdanau describes developing soft alignment to avoid an encoder-decoder bottleneck and says it was independent of Neural Turing Machines, Memory Networks and some earlier cognitive-science work. He does not name Schmidhuber. That account explains his mechanism's origin but is not a point-by-point answer to the 1990-93 priority claim.

agreed_facts: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio posted 'Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate' on arXiv on 1 September 2014, and the paper cites Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's 1997 LSTM paper but not Schmidhuber's 1991-93 attention work.
Schmidhuber and Huber's 'Learning to generate artificial fovea trajectories for target detection' appeared in the International Journal of Neural Systems in 1991, based on a 1990 technical report.
Larochelle and Hinton presented 'Learning to combine foveal glimpses with a third-order Boltzmann machine' at NIPS 2010, and its reference list does not include Schmidhuber and Huber.
Mnih et al. posted 'Recurrent Models of Visual Attention' on arXiv in June 2014, citing Larochelle and Hinton (2010) and Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997).
The ACM's announcement of 27 March 2019 says Bengio's group 'introduced a form of attention mechanism which led to breakthroughs in machine translation'.
crux: The dispute is over whether sequential, learned focusing of a network on selected parts of its input, as in the 1990-93 systems, is the same idea as the 2010 glimpse model and the 2014 alignment mechanism. The alternative is that the later systems differ enough in what is learned and how, for example in the softmax alignment over encoder states. A related question is whether the later authors knew of the earlier work, which the linked sources do not settle.
